Argos. One of the oldest cities in Greece, located in the northeastern Peloponnese, it was a major Mycenaean power and later a rival to Sparta. Though politically overshadowed by stronger neighbors, Argos maintained lasting cultural significance throughout the ancient world.

This is the legendary birthplace of Heracles, the greatest of the Greek heroes, born to Alcmene and Zeus in the palace of Amphitryon. During the Trojan War, Argos was ruled by Diomedes, a fierce warrior second only to Achilles, who fought valiantly against Troy's forces and even stood against gods on the battlefield.

The city was home to the Heraion, the Temple of Hera, one of the earliest and greatest Doric temples, built around 500 BCE. Inside stood a renowned statue by Polycletus. According to legend, the city itself was founded by Danaus, a figure fleeing Egypt with his fifty daughters, who established the city and the dynasty that produced kings and heroes throughout Greek history.

Argos was a center for bronze-working and craftsmanship, producing high-quality pottery and metal goods that were traded throughout the Mediterranean. It stood as a rival to the nearby city of Sparta, located in the same region but politically opposed, leading to periodic conflicts over regional dominance.

The name Argive appears throughout Greek literature as a term used broadly for Greeks themselves. Argive soldiers in Homer's poetry refer to Greeks in general. Heracles was born at Argos, and Diomedes, the great Argive warrior, achieved glory at Troy.
